title: Ansel and the Cellar
premise: Oscar Galloway returns to Hollow Creek as a new teacher, only to discover the school has a missing-class problem and that her childhood imaginary friend, Ansel, is waiting on her porch—unchanged after twenty years and no longer imaginary. As students vanish and the old well beneath the schoolhouse begins to refill, Oscar learns the founders' ritual was never finished and that her family's inheritance binds her to it. Torn between loyalty to Ansel, who has been protecting her all along, and the terrible truth that Ansel is the ritual's unfinished half, Oscar must complete the founders' work—naming and releasing Ansel—before the well refills and takes the whole town. She finishes the ritual at cost: Ansel dissolves into the sealed well, and Oscar, finally knowing who she is, stays to teach in the quiet that follows.
about_author: Beatrix Delacroix is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent a decade collecting the folk rituals of Appalachian mining towns before turning them into fiction. She writes horror that treats small communities with tenderness and their secrets without mercy.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: Oscar Galloway's POV. Oscar arrives in Hollow Creek to teach fourth grade, unpacking in her late grandmother's house, and finds Ansel—her childhood imaginary friend—waiting on the porch, unchanged. The emotional beat is uncanny homecoming: relief curdling into dread as Oscar realizes she never stopped hearing the noises she spent ten years explaining away.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. On her first day, a boy mentions his sister's class 'went down' last spring, and the principal's records show a missing class every nineteen years, papered over. Oscar's rationalizations fray. The beat is institutional wrongness—smiling staff, sealed stairwell, a roster with her own grandmother's name on it.

chapters.title: What Ansel Knows
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, with Ansel's dialogue. Ansel admits she has been holding something shut beneath the school since before Oscar was born, but refuses to say what, warning that knowing is how the well 'tastes you.' The beat is loyalty tested: Oscar wants truth; Ansel wants to protect her, and both are right to be afraid.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In the county archive, Oscar finds the founders' ledger: a ritual begun in 1887 to bind something in the well, requiring a 'named heir' to finish it—every heir so far has died or fled. Her grandmother's page is torn out. The beat is inheritance as burden, and the first appearance of the well refilling early.

chapters.title: Nineteen Years
chapters.summary: Alternating Oscar and the principal, Marlowe Voss's POV. Voss confesses the school board has fed the well a class every nineteen years to keep it quiet, and offers Oscar a place in the arrangement. The beat is complicity: decent people doing monstrous arithmetic, and Oscar realizing her hiring was not an accident.

chapters.title: Down the Stairwell
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A student, Denny, follows the humming to the sealed stairwell and is taken. Descending against Ansel's pleas, Oscar sees the well half-full of black water and hears the voices of every missing class—still reciting lessons. The beat is horror made intimate: the missing are not dead, they are kept.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, flashback-heavy. Reconstructing her grandmother's torn page, Oscar learns Ansel is not a guardian but the ritual's unfinished half—the founders' first offering, given a child's shape and a child's love so no heir could bear to finish it. The beat is devastating truth: the friend who loves her is the lock, and the key.

chapters.title: Refilling
chapters.summary: Multiple POV—Oscar, Voss, Denny's mother. The well rises fast now; lights fail across town, and the kept voices grow loud enough for everyone to hear. Voss tries to force a hasty, botched ritual with a kidnapped child. The beat is panic and moral collapse as the town's long bargain comes due at once.

chapters.title: The Naming
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the well's edge, Oscar rejects both Voss's sacrifice and Ansel's plea to flee, and instead performs the founders' true rite: speaking Ansel's original name—the founders' daughter's name—acknowledging her, and letting her go. The climax is grief and love fused; the well drains as Ansel unravels, singing the lullaby she taught Oscar first.

chapters.title: Quiet
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, weeks later. The missing are released as memory rather than return; the town mourns honestly for the first time in a century, and Oscar keeps teaching, the stairwell bricked and silent. On the last day of school, chalk writes one word in her handwriting she doesn't remember writing: 'stay.' The beat is bittersweet resolution with a single unresolved breath.
